title: 1/f frequency noise in mechanical resonators scales inversely with volume, not with quality factor
abstract: Mechanical frequency-shift sensors have never reached their fundamental thermomechanical or quantum limits. Every material, size, and transduction scheme yet examined yields a $1/f$ floor 1-3 orders higher, with a flicker-noise coefficient $h_{-1} \propto 1/V_{\varepsilon}$. Surveying the published record, I find the invariant $h_{-1}\,V_{\varepsilon} \equiv σ_A ^2\, V_{\varepsilon}/(2\ln 2)$ independent of device size across 13 decades; volume-independent noise is excluded by 9$σ$, site-averaging by 3.8$σ$. No $Q$ dependence appears: reported $Q^{-n}$ laws scale equivalently when $Q$ and volume co-vary; only volume scaling survives when they do not. Mass resolution follows as $|δm| \propto \sqrt{h_{-1}\,V_{\varepsilon} \cdot V}$.
summary: This paper investigates the fundamental limits of frequency stability in mechanical resonators, finding that the dominant $1/f$ noise floor scales universally with the material and geometry, independent of the device's physical volume. The research establishes a key invariant quantity that suggests the noise is governed by intrinsic material properties rather than simple geometric scaling. This has implications for designing next-generation, ultra-sensitive quantum sensors.
main_problem: Mechanical frequency-shift sensors are limited by a persistent, high $1/f$ noise floor that exceeds fundamental thermomechanical or quantum limits.
main_result: The excess $1/f$ noise floor, characterized by the product $h^{-1} V_{\epsilon}$, is found to be remarkably independent of the device's physical volume over many decades of size.
method: The study analyzes a large dataset of mechanical resonators, fitting the scaling of the noise floor ($\sigma_A$) against device volume ($V$) and comparing results against theoretical scaling predictions.
model_or_system: The system involves mechanical resonators (NEMS/MEMS) whose frequency shifts are monitored. The noise is modeled as arising from an ensemble of fluctuating defects (fluctuators) within the material.
key_observables: The excess $1/f$ frequency noise ($\sigma_A$), characterized by the Allan deviation plateau $\sigma_A \propto h^{-1}$, and the invariant product $h^{-1} V_{\epsilon}$.
important_parameters: Device volume ($V$), strain-weighted volume integral ($V_{\epsilon}$), Quality Factor ($Q$), and the noise scaling exponent ($p$).
main_assumptions: The noise is assumed to originate from an ensemble of fluctuators with log-uniformly distributed correlation times, and that the noise plateau is parametric in origin.
figures_summary: Figures plot the $1/f$-floor noise versus participation volume, demonstrating a volume-invariant trend, and analyze scaling trends against theoretical predictions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of noise limitation, surveys existing data to test scaling laws (volume vs. Q), derives the volume-invariant scaling law, and discusses the implications for mass resolution and noise cancellation techniques.
why_interesting: While focused on classical mechanics and materials science, the analysis of noise sources, scaling laws, and fundamental limits of measurement precision touches upon concepts of decoherence and noise floor characterization relevant to quantum sensing.
